Triggers.value: A specific temperature on the skin
A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
Any form of physical contact with others

Threat.value: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly

Negative Appraisals.value: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
I am permanently an outsider now

issues.item: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
issues.explanation: The social avoidance items are difficult to reconcile with the stated trauma type of childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. These triggers imply avoidance of people linked to a discrete later-life event, but the trauma is chronic/developmental and caregiver-based; there is no corresponding trigger or appraisal content tying prior social contacts or specific intimacy-linked reminders to the abuse history.

issues.item: Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
issues.explanation: Intrusion Monitoring suggests fear of an intruder entering the home, which fits home-invasion or stalking trauma better than childhood caregiver physical abuse. With no accompanying memory or trigger content about nighttime entry, footsteps, doors, or home intrusion, this threat item is hard to explain from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: No Good Ahead and Outsider are broad, depressive or social-identity appraisals, whereas the other active content is dominated by vigilance, bodily threat detection, and sensory triggering. This combination is not impossible, but here the intimacy/social avoidance items appear to depend on relational shame or alienation that is otherwise underdeveloped and weakly connected to the trigger/threat pattern, reducing coherence.

issues.item: No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore
issues.explanation: Given the formulation, Triggers and Negative Appraisals should be tightly linked, but the chosen triggers are mainly tactile/somatic/intrusive-memory cues while two maladaptive strategies focus on avoiding social contacts and intimacy. Those strategies are not well supported by the trigger set and feel targeted at a different symptom cluster than the one represented elsewhere.

vignette:
# Marcus

Marcus was sixty-six years old when he first described the cold to his wife, though he had been running from it for fifty-eight years. The cold itself was not the trauma—it was the herald. When his father's hands came down on him, they came with a particular temperature, a specific shock that had nothing to do with season or weather. His father had kept his hands in ice water in the garage. Marcus remembered the sound of the lid of the cooler closing, the methodical way his father would walk back inside the house, the way his mother would find an errand elsewhere. The beatings happened in the basement, where the concrete stayed cold year-round, where Marcus learned that cold on skin meant pain was coming. He was eight years old the first time, and he was still eight years old every time he felt that temperature again.

In his sixties now, Marcus worked remotely as a senior software engineer for a financial services firm. His home office was climate-controlled to seventy-two degrees precisely. He had not set foot in an office building in three years. When the air conditioning kicked in—a sudden shift, a draft across his arm or neck—his heart would begin to race before his conscious mind had even registered the temperature change. His body knew what his mind was trying to forget. The pounding in his chest would come first, a wild percussion that made him certain something terrible was about to happen, and only then would the thought arrive: *He's coming. He's getting his hands wet. He's coming down the stairs.* The memory would surface whole and unbidden, not as narrative but as sensation—the cold, the helplessness, the smell of motor oil and concrete dust.

These moments had begun to structure his life in ways he no longer questioned. He avoided looking at his own body, had done so for years. In the shower, he kept his eyes fixed on the tile wall or closed them entirely. He did not stand shirtless. The sight of his own skin seemed to trigger the same cascade of alarm that the temperature did, as if his body itself were a threat he needed to monitor and contain. His wife, Patricia, had learned not to touch him without warning. When she reached for his hand or his shoulder, she would announce it first, speak his name, give him time to brace himself. Even so, unexpected contact—a brush against him in the kitchen, her hand on his back as she passed—sent a jolt of alarm through him so acute it left him breathless. His startle response had become legendary in their marriage, a thing they managed around rather than addressed.

The social isolation had accumulated gradually. Friends from their neighborhood, couples they had known for decades, had begun to drift away. Marcus could not bear to see them. The people who had known him before—before this, before the cold, before his body had become a thing that betrayed him—they represented a kind of witness he could not tolerate. To be in their presence was to feel permanently marked, set apart, as though they could see the damage written across him. He had come to believe that people could not be trusted with this knowledge, that his only safety lay in distance. He had stopped accepting dinner invitations. He made excuses. Patricia had stopped making them.

What brought him finally to seek help was a panic attack in his own home, one so severe that Patricia had called an ambulance. The paramedics had touched him without warning—hands on his chest, on his arm—and he had fought them with a strength that shocked them both. Afterward, sitting in the emergency room, cleared of any cardiac event, Marcus had felt something shift. He was sixty-six years old. He had spent nearly six decades running from a man who had died when Marcus was thirty-two. The cold was still coming. His heart was still racing. And he was still, always, waiting for the basement door to open.
